newsitem.title: UK: Lira on home stretch to ERM, market stays long.
newsitem.headline: Lira on home stretch to ERM, market stays long.

text.p: The lira is on the home stretch for re-entry into the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) with traders happy to remain long of Italian assets on the assumption it will go back in one weekend soon.
"It's all down to timing, the budget and when they get the all clear from the EU monetary committee," said David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns.
"The health warning on this is - Don't go home short of BTPs (Italian government bonds) or the lira any weekend between now and Christmas. The lira's down the home straight back into ERM."

Analysts said the main barrier to re-entry was the 1997 budget but as the bulk of it now has approval in the Lower House, the rest is academic. The bill's passage in the Senate is little more than a formality because the government has a sound majority in the upper house.

Although the lira could go back in as early as this weekend, most in the market seem to think one of the following three weekends ahead of the European Union summit of heads of state and government on December 13/14 is more likely.

On September 17, 1992 the EU's monetary committee suspended the lira from the ERM, the day after Britain suspended the pound following a sustained speculative attack against the weaker members of the system.
After this debacle it was decided that a country could not declare its central rate unilaterally and must instead negotiate the rate at a meeting of the EU's monetary committee.

This could be a sticking point because France in particular has made it quite clear that it is unhappy losing out to Italy in terms of its competitive exchange rate, and would rather the lira joined at a higher, not lower rate.

"France feels it has lost a certain amount of tourist trade as a result of the depreciation of the lira and clothing and textile industries have also been hit by the weaker lira," said Gwyn Hacche, senior economist at HSBC Markets.
This means France would be happier to see a figure for the mark/lira central rate in the 900s rather than the 1000 plus that Italian industry would be happier with.
On Friday the lira was trading around 1,006.00 per mark amid a general feeling that the political will to get the lira back in before the December summit will overpower gripes from France.
The market is betting that the central rate will be settled around the 1,000 level.
Even if it is not, analysts say the lira will rally strongly on re-entry because all the associated risk premium will disappear and it will become a very safe forward carry trade for the market.
"That kind of trade is a no-brainer when you are looking at lira yielding around 400 basis points (4%) over marks," said one trader.
A strong rally would be met with howls of anguish from Italian exporters and the Bank of Italy would be under huge pressure to reduce interest rates to rein the lira in.
To reduce volatility within the system analysts say it is better to get rates down before joining, rather than after. This means the market could get a clue to the timing of lira re-entry.
"The Bank of Italy generally changes rates on Friday night after the market is closed," Bear Stearns Brown said.
"So I think there is a very good chance they will cut rates on a Friday night and go in at the weekend."
